Despite numerous statements by the European Parliament in favor of harmonizing social and tax legislation and despite concrete proposals by the Commission to update and simplify the 1971 Regulation 1408/71, it is the ministers of the Member States themselves who block this necessary reform process in the Council and prevent the realization of the internal market for people.

Mr. President, I voted for this report on the Common Fisheries Policy, but I call on the European Parliament, the Council and the Commission to pay more attention to and monitor the aspect mentioned under point 20 of the report, which has been forgotten, namely how and whether pension amounts, levels and conditions in the fishing sector, and in particular in the artisanal fishing sector, are controlled.

Since the community, in accordance with the relevant declaration in Article 5(1) of Annex IX of the International Convention for the Regulation of Whaling, is solely responsible for the conservation and management of fish stocks and is therefore entitled to determine the corresponding rules and provisions, the Commission should make use of this power and also set the exclusive fishing right for Greek fishermen at 12 nautical miles.

The joint resolution on the "Balkan Syndrome" serves only to cloak the criminal policy of NATO and the European Union, which intervened in Yugoslavia under the pretext of defending human rights and thereby caused irreparable human and material damage.

The European Parliament has, of course, consistently behaved towards itself, because - as the war criminal and former NATO Secretary-General and now High Representative of the EU, Javier Solana, pointed out in his speech in cynical words - the European Parliament has consistently demanded military intervention on the Balkans, both in Bosnia and in Kosovo.

. (FR) That the armies of the great powers have known for ten years the harmfulness of depleted uranium ammunition, also for those who use it, only proves that the general staffs treat their own soldiers the same disrespect as the civilian population and the enemy forces.

Since the beginning of the atomic age with World War II, the dangers and precautions to be observed when handling uranium and other radioactive substances are well known, because it is a highly toxic (chemically and radiologically toxic) element if it is inhaled or ingested, which is also genetically dangerous.

The use of this type of weapon by the United States and other NATO countries during the Gulf War, in Bosnia and Kosovo has already caused the death of many soldiers, suffering and deaths among the residents of the bombed areas and the pollution of the environment in the affected regions.

Given the magnitude of the crime against entire civilian populations, it is urgently necessary to identify the main perpetrators of these criminal acts against humanity, to establish their guilt and to condemn them, and to immediately ban the production, testing, use and sale of weapons with depleted uranium, and not just to accept a moratorium.

We all know that these weapons, which were used by NATO in the Gulf War (1991), in Bosnia (1994-95) and in Kosovo (1999), had serious consequences initially for the bombed civilian population, but also for the environment and the NATO military personnel, the Iraqi, Bosnian, Serbian and Kosovar forces.

Mr. President, after all the tragic events in connection with the bombing of Yugoslavia and the revelations about the use of depleted uranium ammunition, it is now urgently necessary to ban this type of weapon, which can have dangerous effects for a long time even after their use and can hit all those who run the risk of coming into contact with them, blind, that is, without any discernible difference.

Similarly important and urgent is to design a comprehensive policy of assistance, prevention and rehabilitation for all the areas in Yugoslavia that are suffering from the consequences of the use of these projectiles, in order to protect public health and the environment, to clean up the soil and water, and to ensure a continuous economic development of the country and the entire region.

Apart from that, the resolution briefly addresses very serious issues in connection with the analysis and necessary research of depleted uranium, but does not address at any point the ongoing efforts to conceal and hide facts, independent, well-known research work, even scientific papers from NATO countries that prove the danger of depleted uranium and precautionary measures that these countries impose on their armed forces.

In conclusion, I would like to express my bewilderment at the political U-turn that has emerged during our discussion. Mr. President, ladies and gentlemen. On behalf of my colleague, Mr. Patten, who has already left for Moscow, I would like to congratulate the Parliament on today's debate, which offers us a valuable opportunity for exchange of views on the upcoming session of the UN Human Rights Commission in Geneva.

I also observed with concern last year that the current Russian leadership - many of whom are former KGB employees who were appointed by President Putin, who himself was a KGB colonel - has shown great enthusiasm in the arrest of so-called British, American, and Russian spies.

For this reason, the Council and the Member States must advocate universal ratification of the most important human rights instruments available to all countries. We also call on the EU to support the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights and other international organizations and NROs in the fight against the suppression of independent media - a point that Lord Bethell has already touched on - as well as to support journalists and writers and urge all states to abolish censorship, protect the right to access official information, and lift restrictions on access to modern information technology, which is often the salvation for oppressed people.

Mr. President, Mr. Vitorino, Mr. Council President, if we are to make a decision on a matter like human rights, we have two options: We can name principles and avoid naming areas, or we can proceed as we have done, namely to name areas and take the risk that some will be forgotten.

In terms of developing countries, we are therefore forced to develop a special strategy for the sanctions so that not only those who we actually wanted to help and who were already suffering before are affected.

Finally, on the subject of expansion, we see the most important thing not just in the takeover of the material common property, but we demand that the emphasis be placed on the ethical Acquis Communautaire, i.e. first and foremost on democracy, respect for human rights and minorities, so that Europe can really be a community of values, in short, a community.

That is why we are reassured by the offer of cooperation that you have made to this Parliament today, especially in the light of your statements, to which Mr Poettering referred just now and which seemed to lead to the conclusion that the Commission was an institution suffering from a large democratic deficit and that this Parliament should be dissolved after the elections of 1999 and the low voter turnout in your country.

Firstly, will the Swedish presidency convene a council or special session to which the representatives of the accession countries will be invited, in order, on the one hand, to advance the negotiations and, on the other hand, to send an important signal to the public that enlargement is not only a political goal, a mirage, a still distant goal, but that we are actually making the necessary progress?

Like some other speakers today, I am also concerned about the tendency to often and emphatically highlight the inter-state model at the expense of the so-called Community Approach, which gives the Commission a stronger role and significance.

If you can convince your fellow citizens that the euro is a good project, that it is stable internally, and that its stability is also getting better externally, if you can convince them to contribute to this great work of European integration, you will also contribute to the fact that this area of the European Union is better understood by the citizens.

Following the agenda is the report (A5-0393/2000) by Mr. Simpson on behalf of the Committee on Regional Policy, Transport and Tourism on the Commission proposal for a regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council amending Council Regulation (EEC) No 3922/91 on harmonizing technical rules and administrative procedures in civil aviation.

However, in the Committee on Regional Policy, Transport and Tourism, it is clear that the trade unions and the aviation companies are best placed to find a solution to this problem, and so the members of the Committee have agreed on a compromise whereby all parties will be given until 1 May 2001 to reach an agreement on which the text of the new section Q will then be based.

That's why I also say very clearly: Although we agree with the report in many parts, we do not consider it appropriate that the Parliament sets its own detailed foundations in certain areas - the keyword "single flight attendant" or the duration of employment, i.e. how long someone has already been a flight attendant - in this regulation.

Mr. President, Mr. Simpson, Mrs. Commissioner! After I just saw the news, I hoped - and actually it looked like that too - that we would have a debate on fox hunting, which will certainly be a very lively debate in the British Parliament tonight.

Although we do not yet have complete and 100% confirmed information about this, we at least recognize the seriousness of the situation and wonder whether we should ask the Commission in this case not to take any action - otherwise we would choose another way - to request certain measures in this area.

Mr. President, Mr. Simpson has really presented an excellent report. I can say that because I am one of the few who not only politically but also professionally are familiar with this sector, because before I turned to my work as a Member of this Parliament, I had about 10,000 flight hours as a member of a cockpit crew.

I draw your attention to the fact that safety is the overriding concern of air traffic, which must be borne in mind, since safety depends on two factors: on the technical factor, that is to say, the equipment, aircraft, airports, radio navigation and air traffic control installations, etc., and on the extremely important human factor, which, although it does not play a decisive role, does play a very high part in aircraft accidents.

I am not speaking as a union representative, but as a passenger who would really like to receive, if not an absolute, at least the greatest possible guarantee that excessive stress on the human factor, which can sometimes have fatal consequences, will be avoided.

Either the parties agree by May, or we expect that the Commission will make a proposal that we can incorporate into the second reading, because it is not acceptable that the decisive question for the safety of passengers, namely, whether the captains, the crews, are sufficiently rested to perform their duties, is not regulated.

Finally, Mr. President, I refer to the need to help the Commission in its work on this very complex area, and to the priority of creating the European Aviation Safety Agency, as well as to the urgently needed independent regulation on the issues of rest periods for crew members, which we are currently dealing with.

Based on this, the proposed amendment to the existing regulation aims at achieving a twofold objective: On the one hand, it aims at further harmonizing the regulatory system in the field of civil aviation safety by extending it to the harmonization of operational requirements for aircraft; on the other hand, it aims at defining procedures that will enable the Community to deal with the variations and exceptions that Member States have to apply from time to time for operational reasons.

The amendments 9 and 10 can be accepted without change, but amendments 6, 7, 8 and 11 should be revised in their wording, as we now accept them - as well as amendments 12, 13 and 17 - only in principle and with a revision.

Regarding the specific problem of thrombosis - which someone of you has mentioned - the Commission has written to the air transport companies to inform passengers about the dangers, predisposing factors, and measures to minimize these risks, specifically in relation to thrombosis and general health problems.

Following the agenda is the report (A5-0381/2000) by Mrs Hedkvist Petersen on behalf of the Committee on Regional Policy, Transport and Tourism on the Commission Communication to the Council, the European Parliament, the Economic and Social Committee and the Committee of the Regions: Priorities for road safety in the EU - Progress report and classification of measures.

Let me, Madam Commissioner, make one more brief remark: In my view, it is extremely impolite towards our Parliament that, in advance of our debate tonight, in which we are discussing a regulation on the maximum permissible blood alcohol level, the Commission member has now apparently already decided that a recommendation to the Member States is sufficient.

Let's create regulations, seek a greater degree of harmonization, promote measures to shape pedestrian and bicycle traffic reasonably and safely, and seek formulas to reduce heavy truck traffic, at least in the towns; harmonize speed limits through an ambitious legal framework, as proposed by the Commission in 1986, by waking up the Member States from their inertia.

In my opinion, it becomes clear here that traffic safety cannot be increased to the required extent with individual measures, but that this can only be achieved through a whole range of measures, and this includes traffic education, speed limits, alcohol limits, better road construction, traffic control systems, higher safety standards for vehicles, stronger enforcement of the Road Traffic Act and also a permanent inspection of vehicles in traffic.

For this reason, I also regret very much that the amendment to harmonize the re-registration of accident vehicles in the European Union was not adopted, although independent reports clearly demonstrate a substantial link between once accident vehicles and increased risk of death in subsequent accidents.

And of course, we must also activate and strengthen local communities and regional authorities on issues of road safety to get closer to the people, while the information offensive must continue with - if you will - smarter methods to address the public and especially young people.

What good is the regret that 95% of traffic accidents on the roads and thus only a very small part on rail and air transport occur, if the policy of all governments consists in openly or de facto favoring the car over all other modes of transport for passenger or freight transport.

Mr. President, road safety can and must be a priority for Europe as a whole and for each individual country. Therefore, I also support the proposal by Mrs. Hedkvist Petersen - to which I would like to congratulate her on her report at this point - to design a strategic plan for road safety and to set a number of strict, but also realistic quantitative targets.

In addition, other proposals mentioned in the report, such as stronger support for the European program for the assessment of new vehicles, the promotion of campaigns for the use of seat belts, the development of telematics systems, and the mandatory installation of daytime running lights in motorcycles and vehicles, can be implemented relatively cheaply with high benefits for road traffic safety and public health.

First, no EU state would accept if another member state were to tolerate a flight captain drinking alcohol in a plane with 300 passengers, a ship captain responsible for the safety of 1,000 people, or a train driver drinking alcohol before taking responsibility for his passengers.

Information campaigns on best practices in the EU states and mandatory measures to reduce accident causes such as alcohol, drug use and medication intake, but also a directive that promotes the creativity of the automotive industry by expanding safety tests or promoting the program for evaluating new vehicles, Euro-NCAP, can prove this.

Mr. President, first of all, I would like to sincerely congratulate Mrs. Hedkvist Petersen on her comprehensive resolution proposal, which she has developed for road safety and demonstrates the interest of the European Parliament - which has also been shown in your speeches today - in an ambitious policy to combat the evil of road accidents.

I would like to emphasize that I am in full agreement with the content of the report and its conclusion, the resolution, both with regard to the current action programme, which is about to come to an end, and with regard to the future programme on road safety, for which the Commission has planned a proposal for the coming months.

In the first stage, the last priority measures that were established within the current program on road safety must be implemented. In particular, it is proposed that the obligation to install speed limiters be applied to a larger number of heavy goods vehicles, by including vehicles with lower load capacity.

In a second stage, a more systematic approach must be developed with a view to the future action program, by setting quantitative targets at the European level. Their development must be carried out with the involvement of the Member States in order to achieve a higher effectiveness and complementarity between the measures set by Brussels and those established at the national level.

Secondly, there are habits, customs, reasons that lead me to the conclusion that this is the classic issue that should remain in the area of subsidiarity, and therefore we are only making a recommendation of 0.5. I assume that you have a different point of view - I have noticed that - and it is of course a fact that there has not been sufficient majority in the Council so far to bring such an initiative forward.

I want to say that we have not rejected regulations on front structures that are less dangerous for people, for unprotected bodies, but we simply want to be more effective by winning the support of the automotive sector.

Following the agenda is the report (A5-0358/2000) by Mrs. Poli Bortone on behalf of the Committee on Regional Policy, Transport and Tourism on the Commission's communication to the European Parliament, the Council and the Economic and Social Committee on the implementation of the action programme laid down in the Communication on Intermodality and Intermodal Freight Transport in the European Union.

When analyzing the friction costs in intermodal freight transport in detail, it is found that the main problem points compared to the traditional unimodal transport are higher prices, longer travel times, increasing average distances traveled by goods, quality reduction, greater risk of damage, restrictions on the type of goods transported, and more complex administrative procedures.

Finally, a series of obstacles caused by the lack of harmonization of deadlines and schedules between individual transport modes characterizes the entire system, leading to inconsistencies between the requirements associated with the goods transport chain and the operational requirements of the resources used in the process: For example, the working hours of drivers and crews are not aligned with intermodal operations and terminals cannot always adapt to the 24-hour schedules of train and ship plans.

In its report "Intermodality and Intermodal Freight Transport in the European Union", the Commission has shown the targets to be achieved in intermodal transport and has divided them into three priority intervention areas, so-called key actions, according to the specific problems. The first key action concerns the integration of infrastructure and transport means, the second the interoperability and the joint operation and the third the transport mode-independent services and regulations.

The goal is to establish an information system that will enable real-time traffic management and the use of electronic transactions in freight transport, and this will be achieved through the following measures: Development of intermodal electronic real-time transaction and information systems; Harmonization of communication standards, procedures, and transport documents based on EDI; Unification of liability regulations with the aim of providing customers with a clear regulatory framework of transparent liability conditions and procedures for damaged or lost freight; Development of information society technologies for the benefit of intermodal transport by creating an open system architecture that enables intermodal location and tracking (tracking and tracing); Facilitation of paperless transport through

The Commission communication and the report have brought up many, indeed all, of the key issues. The revision of the trans-European networks to a truly intermodal network, measures to create a logistics added value, harmonizations that are still needed on loading units and other more, truly intermodal information, standardized notifications and documents, promotion of intermodal liability rules and much more.

Regarding the issue of intermodality in crossing the Alps, it should be noted that, apart from the decision of Switzerland in favor of significant investments in the railway sector, there is a worrying backlog in the construction of other transport axes and new railway tunnels, which were already planned by the Community, such as the Turin-Lyon-Brenner axis, or in the discussion, such as the Aosta-Martigny axis.

The contribution we are making therefore has two consequences that I would like to highlight: First, if we, thanks to the methodology that we hope to receive and accept from the Commission, achieve a clearer definition and allocation of internal and external costs to users, we will create the conditions for the financing of the infrastructure, which is currently guaranteed by the public sector or through general taxation, to be shifted to users as such.
